questions.q: Why does the lesson say a `team` tag spelled three different ways (`payments`, `Payments`, `pay-team`) breaks cost allocation, even though every resource technically has a tag?
options: Azure Policy automatically deletes resources with inconsistent tag casing
AWS Cost Explorer ignores any tag key longer than four characters
It only matters for tags on storage resources, not compute
The inconsistent values don't group into one bucket in Cost Analysis or Cost Explorer — they fragment into three separate buckets
questions.explain: Grouping by tag only works when the tag's value is written consistently; different spellings of what should be the same value split one team's spend across multiple unrelated buckets.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what matters more than the exact set of tag keys an organization chooses?
options: Consistency — every resource actually carrying the small set of keys chosen, with values drawn from a fixed list
Using the maximum number of tag keys AWS or Azure technically allows
Renaming tag keys every fiscal quarter to match the current org chart
Applying tags only to production resources and skipping staging and dev entirely
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that five keys every resource actually carries beats twenty keys half the resources are missing — consistency is the thing that makes allocation reliable.

questions.q: In the Azure Policy example in this lesson, what does setting the policy's Effect to Deny accomplish?
options: It sends a weekly email report listing untagged resources
It rejects an attempt to deploy a resource without the required tag at deployment time, rather than flagging it afterward
It automatically renames an incorrectly cased tag to the correct casing
It activates the tag as a Cost Allocation Tag in the Billing console
questions.explain: A Deny effect enforces the tag requirement at the point of deployment — the resource simply can't be created without it, instead of being caught in a later audit.

questions.q: What does an AWS Organizations tag policy do, according to this lesson?
options: Replaces the need for AWS Cost Explorer entirely
Automatically negotiates Reserved Instance pricing with AWS
Defines which tag keys are required, which capitalization is enforced, and which values are allowed, for accounts in an OU
Converts Azure Policy definitions into an equivalent AWS format
questions.explain: A tag policy attached to an organizational unit or organization specifies required keys, enforced capitalization, and allowed values, then reports or prevents violations.

questions.q: What is the difference the lesson draws between enforcing a tag's existence and activating it as a Cost Allocation Tag in AWS?
options: There is no difference — enforcing a tag automatically activates it for Cost Explorer
Activation only applies to Azure, never to AWS
Enforcing a tag's existence happens in IAM, while activation happens in EC2
They are two separate steps — a tag policy can require the tag exist, but it still must be separately activated in Billing before Cost Explorer can group or filter by it
questions.explain: Even a perfectly enforced tag won't appear as a grouping option in Cost Explorer until an administrator activates it as a Cost Allocation Tag in the Billing console — a distinct, separate step.
